title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: twofold hate — vengeance vs less love; Vasquez; Leah
pass_a_gloss: Lastly (which directly breaks the nerves of this argument) I say that God can be said to have hated Esau in a twofold respect: Either to have hated unto vengeance and the punishment of eternal death to be inflicted upon him: and thus he does not hate Esau except as a sinner, and on account of the sin itself, as the moving and demeritorious cause of this hatred: Or to have hated Esau unto the negation of some special and unowed benefit, that is, to have loved less: and thus he can hate Esau only because he does not will to love him. In this latter sense God is said by the Apostle to have loved Jacob and hated Esau, because according to the freest purpose of his will he willed to soften Jacob by special grace; but he did not will to affect Esau with this so great benefit. If here it be asked why he chose Jacob unto this special grace, and not Esau, it is answered, Because God so willed. If it be asked why he so willed, the question is foolish, because a cause is sought of the Divine will in preparing and distributing its gratuitous goods, of which there is none besides its own cause. But now that the vocabulary of hatred is used for the mere negation of special love in conferring a special benefit, the Jesuits themselves do not deny. Vasquez, looking back to these very words of the Apostle, To hate, says he, is the same as to have loved less. For he bears himself after the manner of one hating, who does not grant to another some gift which he gives to one. Thus such hating does not require sin as the cause of this hatred. In this sense Jacob is said to have held Leah in hatred, Gen. 29:31.
pass_b_english: Lastly — and this breaks the nerve of the argument — God may be said to have hated Esau in two respects. First, hated unto vengeance and the punishment of eternal death: so he hates Esau only as a sinner, and for sin itself as moving and demeritorious cause. Second, hated unto denial of some special unowed benefit — that is, loved less: so he can hate Esau only because he does not will to love him. In that latter sense the Apostle says God loved Jacob and hated Esau: by the freest purpose of his will he chose to soften Jacob by special grace, and refused Esau that great benefit. Why choose Jacob for that grace and not Esau? Because God so willed. Why so will? A foolish question — you seek a cause of the divine will in preparing and distributing gratuitous goods beyond the will itself. That hatred here means mere denial of special love in conferring a special benefit, even the Jesuits grant. Vasquez on these very words: to hate is the same as to have loved less. He acts like one who hates who gives a gift to one and withholds it from another. Such hatred needs no sin as its cause. So Jacob is said to have hated Leah (Gen. 29:31).
source_text: Postremo (quod directe nervos hujus argumenti elidit) dico Deum posse dici odisse Esavum duplici respectu: Vel odisse ad vindictam et poenam aeternae mortis illi infligendam: atque sic non odit Esavum nisi qua peccatorem, et propter ipsum peccatum, ut hujus odii causam motivam et demeritoriam: Vel odisse Esavum ad specialis alicujus et indebiti beneficii negationem, hoc est minus dilexisse: et sic potest odisse Esavum, tantum quia non vult eum diligere. Hoc sensu posteriore dicitur Deus ab Apostolo dilexisse Jacobum et odisse Esavum, quia pro liberrimo voluntatis suae proposito voluit Jacobum emollire per specialem gratiam; noluit autem hoc tanto beneficio afficere Esavum. Si hic quaeratur quare elegit Jacobum ad hanc specialem gratiam, et non Esavum, respondetur, Quia Deus sic voluit. Si cur quaeratur quare sic voluerit, stulta est quaestio, quia Divinae voluntatis in bonis suis gratuitis praeparandis et distribuendis quaeritur causa, cujus nulla est praeter suam causam. Jam vero quod odii vocabulum usurpatur pro sola negatione specialis amoris in speciali beneficio conferendo, non diffitentur ipsi Jesuitae. Vasques ad haec ipsa verba Apostoli respiciens, Odisse, inquit, idem est quod minus dilexisse. Habet enim se ad modum odientis, qui aliquod donum quod uni dat, alteri non concedit. Sic tale odisse non requirit peccatum ut causam hujus odii. Hoc sensu Jacob dicitur odio habuisse Leam, Gen. xxix. 31.
